info.name: OAN API — publish, discover, select
info.description:
The whole stack from Postman: the registry writes that set it up, updates for the fields that change, the reads that show what is there, and the three flows that use it.

ONE FOLDER PER CAPABILITY. Inside each, Publish seeds the catalogue Discover looks for, so run a folder top to bottom the first time; after that any request works on its own.

THERE ARE NO REGISTRY REQUESTS HERE, deliberately. The registry has no route through the gateway and publishes on loopback only, so nothing in a shared collection could reach it. bin/setup.py seeds all of it -- seven participants and all four capability bindings -- from the same .env the adapter configs are rendered from, which is what keeps the two from disagreeing.

NOTHING HERE CHANGES THE STACK ON A DEFAULT RUN. The creates report "already present" once setup.py has run, because the registry is append-only. The updates write back the same values the variables already hold -- edit a variable to actually change a row.

THE UPDATES NEED A SCHEMA THAT PERMITS THEM. The registry re-validates the merged document on update, and that document carries its own osid and osUpdatedAt, so additionalProperties: false rejects the registry's own fields. Participant and ProviderSchema in config/registry/schemas/ must allow additional properties, and the registry reads schemas only at startup.

Every URL here is loopback, because the deployment publishes these ports on the VM's loopback only and nothing else is routable. Open a tunnel first and the defaults work unchanged:

    ssh -L 9202:127.0.0.1:9202 -L 9200:127.0.0.1:9200 \
        -L 8081:127.0.0.1:8081 -L 8080:127.0.0.1:8080 -N you@the-vm

No VM hostname or address appears in this file.

item.name: 1. WeatherObservation

request.description:
Enters at the PROVIDER adapter, which signs it as itself and forwards to the network layer; the network layer verifies that signature and hands it to the discovery service. Posting straight at the discovery service would skip both adapters, and so skip the part worth testing.

context.action is catalog/publish, the name the Beckn v2 spec gives this action at /catalog/publish. A bare "publish" is not a spec action. The callback is catalog/on_publish.

The caller signs nothing and the body names no party: identity travels in the Authorization header's keyId, from the adapter's own keyManager config.

The catalogue carries no offers -- nothing requires them, and select does not read them: it carries its own offer in the request.

Text search across published catalogs.

Route: **exp adapter → network adapter → discovery service.** No provider plugin is involved, and no upstream API is called. The answer comes from the discovery service's own index.

Returns the catalog published in step 3. An empty list almost always means `networkId` or `domain` did not match what was published.

request.description:
Asks for a priced quote on the resource discover returned.

Route: **exp adapter → provider adapter → mock IMD.** This is where the plugins do their work:

1. `validateSign` verifies the caller's key, fetched from the registry — the row you saw in step 1
2. the provider plugin builds the binding key from the payload, asks the registry for the call plan — the row from step 2 — resolves the coordinates, calls the upstream, and maps the answer back
3. `signAck` signs the answer

**The answer is the HTTP response — there is no callback.** A bare `ACK` here would mean nothing served the request; the adapter now returns `404 NET_ENTITY_NOT_FOUND` in that case rather than pretending to accept it.

The response quotes **one** resource, carrying the id this request selected, and follows the same schema pack in `informationMode: Direct` — which requires `observationType`, `source`, `location`, `generatedAt` and `parameters`.

**Two fields here are not in the pack, both deliberately.** The pack carries one validity and one flat `parameters` array per resource, so it cannot express a five-day forecast in the one resource the request selected — hence `observations`. And its parameter entry is `parameter`/`value`/`unit` only, so `aggregation` is ours, because this provider reports a minimum *and* a maximum for temperature and humidity. Both validate: the pack sets no `additionalProperties`.

item.description:
The weather capability end to end: publish its catalogue, find it, then ask for a forecast.

RUN IN ORDER the first time -- Publish seeds the catalogue Discover looks for. After that Select works on its own.

Select is the interesting one. It goes to the same endpoint on the same adapter as Mandi's, and a different domain package answers it: each provider step builds a binding key from the payload, serves the request if the key is its own, and passes it through untouched if not. A 404 NET_ENTITY_NOT_FOUND here means no step claimed this payload -- compare {{providerId}} and the capability @type against the bindings in Registry.

item.name: 2. MandiPrice

request.description:
The second catalogue, entering the same way as the first: the provider adapter signs it and the network layer forwards it to discovery. Publishing is capability-agnostic -- no provider step runs, and nothing on this path knows what a MandiPrice is.

The resource is OnDemand, which is what a catalogue entry should be: it advertises the commodities and price fields this provider CAN answer for. The pack forbids `prices` in that mode, so a catalogue cannot carry stale numbers -- those appear only in the Direct answer to a select, request 8.

request.description:
The same endpoint as request 5, the same adapter, a different capability. Nothing routes this: the payload's provider id and resourceAttributes @type form a binding key, the mandi step recognises it and the weather step passes it through.

The answer is a Direct openagrinet:MandiPrice per price record. Its prices arrive from the upstream as STRINGS with Title Case keys containing spaces, so the mapping converts them; and a record that reported no minimum or maximum must come back with those absent rather than zeroed, which is what the last assertion checks.

The upstream's credential is a query parameter, which the adapter adds from an environment variable and redacts from the URL it logs.

item.description:
The mandi capability end to end: publish its catalogue, find it, then ask for prices.

RUN IN ORDER the first time -- Publish seeds the catalogue Discover looks for.

Nothing here is shared with Weather except the adapter, the registry client and the mapper. A different upstream, a different mapping, a different binding key. The mapping is doing more work than weather's: it converts ISO dates to the dd-MM-yyyy Agmarknet wants, sends marketcode only when the request carried one, turns price strings into numbers, and omits a price that was not reported rather than sending a zero.

request.description:
The same endpoint and the same adapter as the two folders above, a third capability. Nothing routes it: the payload's provider id and resourceAttributes @type form a binding key, the KnowledgeAdvisory step recognises it and the other two pass it through.

THERE IS NO PUBLISH OR DISCOVER HERE, unlike the folders above, and that is the point of informationMode OnDemand. Weather and mandi publish a catalogue that discover then searches. An advisory is retrieved when asked for -- there is no catalogue to seed and nothing to discover, so select is the whole flow.

WHAT COMES BACK. One Direct openagrinet:KnowledgeAdvisory per retrieved passage, each carrying its own text, the section heading it sits under, and the document it came from. One resource per passage rather than one per query is what keeps a passage from being attributed to another document's source.

The request half sends the topic as the provider's query. Everything in the answer is read from what the provider returned -- a field it leaves empty comes back empty rather than filled in from the request.

THIS IS THE ONLY CAPABILITY HERE THAT CALLS A REAL EXTERNAL PROVIDER. The other two are mocks inside the compose network. So this one needs egress from the stack, and it is the only one that can fail because a credential is missing: it authenticates with OAuth2 client credentials, named in the adapter config as environment variables and never held as values in a config file or in the registry.

item.description: The knowledge capability: retrieval from a real external provider, answered on demand. One request, because OnDemand has no catalogue to publish and nothing to discover.

request.description:
The fourth capability on the same adapter and the same endpoint, served by POCRA. Like knowledge it is a real external provider and a single select -- informationMode OnDemand, so there is no catalogue to publish and nothing to discover. Unlike every other capability here it needs NO credential.

THIS IS THE ONE THAT FANS OUT. POCRA's search takes exactly ONE facility type per call: a comma-separated pair answers 200 with no providers and an array is refused, both measured against the live API. So the step splits a payload naming N types into N calls and merges the answers. To see that, add a second entry to supportedFacilityTypes -- "Warehouse" or "SoilTestingFacility" -- and the provider adapter's log will show two calls for one request.

One type is the default deliberately, because each type is another call and POCRA rate-limits.

EACH CALL CARRIES ITS OWN message_id, derived in the mapping from the caller's. That is not tidiness: POCRA caches on message_id for ten minutes and IGNORES location, so reusing one id across the calls returns facilities from wherever it was first asked -- verified 350 km apart. A type filter cannot catch that, because the type still matches.

WHY AN EMPTY ANSWER IS NOT A FAILURE HERE. After roughly twenty calls in a few minutes POCRA starts answering 200 with an empty catalogue, recovering after a pause. That is indistinguishable from "no facility nearby", so the assertions log it rather than failing. It is a known correctness gap, not a quirk of this request.

The coordinates are Ahmednagar, Maharashtra, which is inside POCRA's coverage.

item.description: Agriculture facilities from POCRA, answered on demand and without a credential. One request, and the only capability whose single select can become several upstream calls.

variable.description: Takes unsigned requests -- the app is inside the trust boundary.

Used by no request here, on purpose. Discover reaches this adapter through the experience adapter and publish through the provider adapter. It is listed because it is the other adapter a deployment exposes, and both its /publish and /discover verify signatures -- so a network peer calls it directly. Postman does not sign, so those calls are not scripted.
